results.result: Prior work established that primate V2 contains a repeating pale-thin-pale-thick stripe pattern of cytochrome oxidase (CO) activity, forming a columnar system with distinct functional properties. Thin stripes are sensitive to color and project to V4, while thick stripes are sensitive to binocular disparity and project to MT. In macaques, stripes have a center-to-center distance of ~4.0 mm and widths of 0.7-1.3 mm, approximately doubled in humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Tootell and Hamilton, 1989; Shipp and Zeki, 1985; Tootell et al., 1983; Hockfield et al., 1990; Tootell and Taylor, 1995; Adams et al., 2007). These claims establish the foundational knowledge about V2 stripe organization and are consistently reported across multiple studies.

results.result: Prior histological studies using myelin staining techniques showed inconsistent results regarding the correspondence between CO activity and myelin density in V2 stripes. Luxol fast blue indicated stronger myelination in thin/thick stripes, while Gallyas silver staining showed pale stripes being more myelinated. These discrepancies were replicated across studies, and all standard histochemical methods are highly sensitive to specimen condition and procedural variations.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C13 are supported by citations to relevant histological studies (Tootell et al., 1983; Krubitzer and Kaas, 1989; Horton and Hocking, 1997; Savaskan et al., 2009). The authors accurately describe the inconsistencies in prior histological findings, which provides important context for why the current qMRI study is needed. The limitations of histochemical methods are appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Quantitative MRI (qMRI) isolates sources of image contrast to create reproducible parameter maps (R1, R2*, PD) in physical units that are less acquisition-dependent. qMRI provides closer relationships to specific microstructural components like myelin and iron, though single parameter maps lack specificity to directly infer single tissue components. Cortical R1 is largely affected by myelin content and has been used as a surrogate to study cortical myelination.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C19 are supported by appropriate citations (Edwards et al., 2018; Trampel et al., 2019; Weiskopf et al., 2021; Lazari and Lipp, 2021; Stüber et al., 2014; Leuze et al., 2017; Sigalovsky et al., 2006; Dick et al., 2012; Sereno et al., 2013; Lutti et al., 2014). The authors appropriately acknowledge both the advantages of qMRI and its limitations, particularly the lack of specificity of single parameters. The relationship between R1 and myelin is well-established in the cited literature.

results.result: Recent ultra-high field fMRI developments enabled functional localization of thin and thick stripes by exploiting their differential sensitivity to color and binocular disparity. Color-selective stripes are largely confined to CO thin stripes, while selectivity for binocular disparity is found in all stripe types but most frequently in CO thick stripes.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C28, and C29 are supported by appropriate citations (Nasr et al., 2016; Dumoulin et al., 2017; Navarro et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2003; Tootell et al., 2004; Peterhans and von der Heydt, 1993; Chen et al., 2008). The authors accurately describe the functional properties of different stripe types and acknowledge that the correspondence is not absolute (disparity selectivity is found in all stripe types but most frequently in thick stripes).

results.result: The study included four healthy participants (1 female, age 27.50 ± 4.39 years) with normal vision who were scanned multiple times at 7T. High-resolution fMRI (0.8 mm isotropic) was used to map color-selective thin stripes and disparity-selective thick stripes in two sessions each. High-resolution anatomical images (0.5 mm isotropic) were acquired using the MPM protocol to derive quantitative parameter maps (R1, R2*, PD).
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 and C70-C75 describe the study design and participant characteristics. These are straightforward methodological details that are clearly stated in the manuscript. The sample size of n=4 is small but appropriate for this type of high-resolution neuroimaging study at 7T. The study was approved by the local ethics committee, and participants met appropriate inclusion criteria.

results.result: Color-selective thin stripes were mapped using isoluminant sinusoidal red/blue or black/white gratings at 0.4 cpd to mitigate chromatic aberration and exploit color selectivity at this spatial scale. Flicker photometry was used to determine isoluminance ratios for each participant. Disparity-selective thick stripes were mapped using overlaid red and green random dot stereograms with maximal disparity of ±0.22°.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C82 describe the visual stimulation paradigms and are supported by appropriate citations (Tootell and Nasr, 2017; Tootell et al., 2004; Li et al., 2019; Nasr et al., 2016; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Bilodeau and Faubert, 1997; Ives, 1907; Bone and Landrum, 2004; Blakemore and Julesz, 1971; Tsao et al., 2003). The methods are well-established and appropriate for the functional localization of V2 stripes. The use of flicker photometry to control for isoluminance is a strength.

results.result: All experiments were performed on a 7T MR scanner with a single-channel transmit/32-channel receive head coil. Functional data was acquired with 2D gradient-echo EPI. MR relaxation parameters were measured with the MPM protocol, with prospective motion correction using an optical tracking system. Whole-brain anatomy was acquired using MP2RAGE for cortex segmentation. Quantitative parameter maps were computed using the hMRI toolbox, and cortex segmentation was performed using FreeSurfer with the equi-volume model for mid-cortical depth sampling.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C92 describe the MRI acquisition and analysis methods and are supported by appropriate citations (Feinberg et al., 2010; Moeller et al., 2010; Vaculčiaková et al., 2022; Marques et al., 2010; Tabelow et al., 2019; Dale et al., 1999; Fischl et al., 1999; Zaretskaya et al., 2018; Waehnert et al., 2014; Wagstyl et al., 2018). The methods are state-of-the-art for high-resolution quantitative neuroimaging at 7T. The use of prospective motion correction is a strength given the long acquisition times and high resolution.

results.result: No activation was found for binocular disparity in V1, consistent with prior findings, while large V1 activation was found for color contrast.
results.evaluation: Claims C30 and C31 are supported by data shown in Figure 2 and citations to Tsao et al., 2003 and Nasr et al., 2016. The findings are consistent with known functional properties of V1, which shows strong responses to color but minimal responses to binocular disparity at the disparity levels used in this study. This serves as a validation of the experimental paradigm.

results.result: Activation maps were consistent between sessions of color and disparity stripe measurements, with statistically significant correlations demonstrated in Figure 3.
results.evaluation: Claim C32 is supported by data shown in Figure 3, which demonstrates statistically significant correlations between sessions for both color-selective and disparity-selective stripe mapping. The use of permutation testing with spatial autocorrelation preservation (BrainSMASH) is appropriate. This demonstrates good test-retest reliability of the functional localization, which is important for the subsequent qMRI analysis.

results.result: R1 maps showed higher values in primary motor and sensory cortical areas, congruent with higher myelin density in these areas. All participants showed increased R1 values in V1 compared to other cortical regions. R1, R2*, and MTVF values decreased toward the pial surface in V2, as expected for myelin-sensitive parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 are supported by data shown in Figures 4 and Appendix 2, with appropriate citations (Flechsig, 1920; Glasser and Van Essen, 2011; Sereno et al., 2013; Mezer et al., 2013; Marques et al., 2017; Carey et al., 2018; Kirilina et al., 2020). These findings validate the qMRI measurements by demonstrating that they reproduce known patterns of cortical myelination across brain regions and cortical depth. This is an important quality control step.

results.result: The study found statistically significant lower R1 values (in the range of 1-2%) in color-selective thin and disparity-selective thick stripes compared to locations containing pale stripe contributions, pointing toward higher myelin density in pale stripes. These results were confirmed using an independent R1 estimate from the MP2RAGE sequence. The coefficient of variation in R1 maps was 11.3 ± 0.7% in V2.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C22, C36, C39, C44, and C46 represent the main findings of the study. The results are supported by data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures, with appropriate statistical testing using permutation analysis. The finding of lower R1 in thin and thick stripes is statistically significant across multiple z-score thresholds and is replicated with an independent R1 measurement method (MP2RAGE). The effect size (1-2%) is small but comparable to R1 differences between cortical areas. The interpretation that lower R1 indicates higher myelin density in pale stripes is based on the established relationship between R1 and myelin (C18), though the authors appropriately acknowledge that R1 is a surrogate marker. The replication with MP2RAGE strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: No consistent differences in R2* were found between stripe types in the main analysis.
results.evaluation: Claim C23 is supported by data shown in Figure 5c-d, which shows no statistically significant differences in R2* between stripe types in the main analysis. The authors provide a reasonable explanation for this null finding (C40-C43), noting that R2* is sensitive to multiple factors including iron, myelin, vasculature, and cortical orientation relative to the magnetic field. The supplementary analysis excluding the foveal region (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) does show some significant R2* differences, suggesting the null result in the main analysis may be due to regional heterogeneity or confounding factors.

results.result: R2* is sensitive to paramagnetic iron and diamagnetic myelin, and other factors like vasculature and cortical orientation to the magnetic field have an influence on R2*, which might have obscured the underlying dependency on myelin content. Higher vessel densities were found in blobs and stripes of squirrel and macaque monkeys, though this was later disputed by another study showing no differences in vascular supply between blobs and inter-blobs in V1.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 provide context for interpreting the R2* results and are supported by appropriate citations (Stüber et al., 2014; Kirilina et al., 2020; Cohen-Adad et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 1991; Keller et al., 2011; Adams et al., 2015). The authors appropriately acknowledge the complexity of R2* as a contrast mechanism and the conflicting evidence regarding vascular differences between CO-rich and CO-poor regions. This discussion strengthens the interpretation of the null R2* finding.

results.result: Missing activation at the representation of the central fovea for both color and disparity stimuli could be due to the macula lutea and absence of blue cones in the central fovea for color stimuli, and eccentricity dependence of disparity tuning for disparity stimuli. A prior study found a similar eccentricity-dependent activation pattern for disparity stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 address a potential limitation of the functional localization. C47 is supported by a citation to Nasr and Tootell, 2018, and provides a reasonable explanation for missing color activation in the fovea. C48 is speculative but reasonable. C49 is supported by a citation to Tsao et al., 2003, which found similar eccentricity-dependent patterns. The authors appropriately address this issue with a supplementary analysis excluding the foveal region (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which confirms the main findings.

results.result: Spatial overlap of activation maps for color-selective thin and disparity-selective thick stripes is expected to some degree due to the limiting physiological point spread function of the BOLD signal in fMRI. Differential contrasts between experimental conditions are known to be less affected by unspecific macrovascular contributions and draining veins.
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C52 address potential confounds in the functional localization. C50 is supported by citations to Polimeni et al., 2010 and Chaimow et al., 2018, and appropriately acknowledges the spatial resolution limits of fMRI. C52 is based on established knowledge in the fMRI field. The authors appropriately excluded overlapping voxels from the ROI definitions, which is a strength of the analysis approach.

results.result: Pistorio et al., 2006 showed in monkey V1 that the edges of blobs are more myelinated rather than blobs or inter-blob regions themselves using a modified Gallyas stain.
results.evaluation: Claim C54 is supported by a citation to Pistorio et al., 2006. The authors appropriately acknowledge this alternative hypothesis that stripe borders rather than stripe centers may be differentially myelinated. However, they note that their methods cannot resolve this question due to spatial resolution limitations. This is an honest acknowledgment of a limitation.

results.result: An optical tracking system was used to prospectively correct head movements during anatomical scans. The equi-volume model was used to sample at mid-cortical depth, which has been shown to be less affected by curvature biases than other models. Remaining curvature contributions were regressed out.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 describe important methodological details for ensuring data quality. C55 addresses motion correction, which is critical for high-resolution imaging. C56-C57 are supported by a citation to Waehnert et al., 2014, and describe the use of an appropriate cortical depth model. C58 is supported by citations to Glasser and Van Essen, 2011; Sereno et al., 2013; Dumoulin et al., 2017, and describes an important correction for cortical curvature effects. These methodological choices are appropriate and strengthen confidence in the results.

results.result: The findings point toward higher myelination of pale stripes, which exhibit lower oxidative metabolic activity according to CO staining. V2 receives most input from V1 and the pulvinar, but pulvinar projections only terminate in layers 3 and 5, whereas the alternating myelin pattern is most obvious in layer 4, which receives input almost exclusively from V1. An anterograde tracer study showed that V1 injections preferentially targeted V2 pale stripes, which might correspond to higher axonal density of V1 to V2 projections in layer 4 of pale stripes, leading to higher myelination in pale stripes.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 provide a mechanistic interpretation of the findings. C59-C62 are supported by appropriate citations (Tootell et al., 1983; Sincich and Horton, 2005). C63 is supported by a citation to Sincich and Horton, 2002. However, C64 and C65 are speculative (as acknowledged by the authors with phrases like "we speculate" and "Although we cannot exclude"). The proposed mechanism linking higher V1 input to pale stripes with higher myelination is plausible but not directly tested in this study. The authors appropriately acknowledge this as speculation, but the interpretation remains uncertain without additional evidence.

results.result: The study demonstrates the feasibility to investigate structure-function relationships in living humans within one cortical area at the level of columnar systems using qMRI. Quantitative R1 values are less biased by technical artifacts and are better comparable among participants and scanner sites. Myelination of cortical areas affects their functional properties (action potential propagation) and correlates with postnatal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C24, C66, and C67 represent the main conclusions of the study. C24 and C66 are supported by the data presented in the manuscript, which successfully combines high-resolution fMRI and qMRI to study myelination differences at the level of V2 stripes. C67 is based on established knowledge about the advantages of qMRI. C68 and C69 are supported by citations to Sanders and Whitteridge, 1946 and Glasser and Van Essen, 2011, and provide broader context for the importance of studying cortical myelination. The conclusion that the study demonstrates feasibility is well-supported, though the small sample size (n=4) and small effect sizes (1-2%) suggest that this approach is technically demanding.

results.result: The BrainSMASH package was used to preserve spatial autocorrelation in spatially shuffled maps for permutation testing.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 describes an important methodological detail for the statistical analysis. The use of BrainSMASH (Burt et al., 2020) to preserve spatial autocorrelation in permutation testing is appropriate and represents a strength of the analysis. Standard permutation tests that do not account for spatial autocorrelation can produce inflated false positive rates in neuroimaging data.
